summary: Describes how Mobile IPv6 Fast Handovers can be carried out on networks using the IEEE 802.16e wireless standard, commonly called mobile WiMAX. It tries to achieve seamless handover by using link-layer handover indicators and lining up the 802.16e steps with the Mobile IPv6 steps. This is an informational document, not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: When a phone moves between towers, the radio part and the internet part must move in step. This explains how to make them work in step on WiMAX, so a switch causes as little interruption as possible.

questions: how does mobile ipv6 work on wimax
subtitle: Making fast handover work on WiMAX networks.

tldr.problem: Mobile IPv6 fast handover (FMIPv6) assumes generic link-layer support, but WiMAX networks have their own handover procedures. Without coordination between the two, handovers are slow and packets are lost.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC describes how to synchronize FMIPv6 and IEEE 802.16e handover procedures using link-layer handover triggers (primitives) and a predictive or reactive mode based on whether the MN receives handover confirmation before switching.
tldr.outcome: Seamless handovers are achieved on WiMAX by letting the IP layer (FMIPv6) and link layer (802.16e) work in concert.

today: RFC 5270 is informational, providing guidance for implementers. It was published in June 2008 as WiMAX was being deployed. Today, WiMAX deployment has declined, but the synchronization principles described in the RFC inform other mobility frameworks and media-independent handover standards like IEEE 802.21.

sections.title: The Handover Problem on WiMAX
sections.content: WiMAX (IEEE 802.16e) is a wireless broadband standard, different from WiFi. Mobile nodes roam between base stations, and when signal strength drops, they initiate handovers. Mobile IPv6 Fast Handover (FMIPv6) is designed to reduce the IP-layer handover latency by allowing the MN to acquire a new address and notify the network before the radio link switches. However, FMIPv6 was written generically. WiMAX has elaborate handover procedures involving neighbor discovery, ranging, and resource allocation. The problem is timing: the IP layer and the link layer do not coordinate, so the MN may lose packets during the gap between when it learns of the new network and when it can route data there.
sections.plainLanguage: WiMAX handover is like changing lanes while driving: you need to check your mirrors, signal, and turn the wheel all at the right moments. FMIPv6 and WiMAX handle these steps separately, causing delays.

sections.title: WiMAX and FMIPv6 Concepts
sections.content:
In WiMAX, a base station periodically broadcasts MOB_NBR-ADV messages listing its neighbors. The mobile node listens, scans candidates, and when signal is good, sends a MOB_MSHO-REQ (handover request). The serving base station replies with MOB_BSHO-RSP (recommended targets). Finally, the MN sends MOB_HO-IND to indicate it is switching.

FMIPv6 uses RtSolPr (router solicitation for proxy advertisement) to learn the new router, FBU (fast binding update) to prepare the network, and FBack (fast binding acknowledgment) as confirmation. The key innovation is triggering FMIPv6 steps using primitives: NEW_LINK_DETECTED signals a new base station was found, LINK_HANDOVER_IMPEND signals the handover is about to execute, and LINK_UP signals the new link is ready.
sections.plainLanguage: WiMAX has its own handover dance: neighbor ads, requests, and replies. FMIPv6 has its own dance: router discovery, address preparation, and acknowledgment. The trick is running both dances in the right order.

sections.title: Synchronized Handover Procedures
sections.content:
The RFC describes a flow in four stages:

Access Router Discovery: When a new WiMAX base station is detected, the link layer triggers NEW_LINK_DETECTED to the IP layer. The IP layer then sends RtSolPr with handover assist information (the new base station ID) to learn which access router serves it.

Handover Preparation: When the MN decides to handover, the link layer triggers LINK_HANDOVER_IMPEND, telling the IP layer the target base station. The IP layer sends FBU to the previous access router (PAR) to set up a tunnel to the new router (NAR). If the MN receives FBack before the link switches, it enters predictive mode (faster recovery).

Handover Execution: The MN switches radio links and performs 802.16e network entry. When link-layer connection is ready, the link layer triggers LINK_UP.

Handover Completion: The IP layer sends an unsolicited neighbor advertisement to the NAR, confirming the new address and triggering packet delivery.
sections.plainLanguage: The steps are: IP layer learns about new tower, decides to move, sends preparation to old router, radio switches, new link comes up, then confirms to new router. Each step signals the next.

sections.title: Predictive and Reactive Modes
sections.content:
Predictive mode occurs when the MN receives FBack before sending MOB_HO-IND to the serving base station. In this case, the serving router already has a tunnel ready, and packets start flowing to the new address even before the radio switches. When the MN arrives at the new base station, buffered packets are immediately available.

Reactive mode occurs if FBack does not arrive before the link switches. The MN sends UNA (unsolicited neighbor advertisement) to the NAR and FBU to the PAR after handover. The PAR and NAR then set up the tunnel. Reactive mode means some packets are lost during the IP-layer handover, but it is still faster than standard Mobile IPv6 because binding updates start immediately upon arrival at the new link.
sections.plainLanguage: Predictive mode is like a relay runner receiving the baton before breaking into a run: no slowdown. Reactive mode is like the runner already running and receiving the baton mid-stride: a short stumble, but still faster than stopping to pick it up.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC notes that primitives between the link layer and IP layer are local to the mobile node, so they do not need external security. However, IEEE 802.16e management messages, especially broadcast MOB_NBR-ADV, are not authenticated. An attacker could forge neighbor advertisements with bogus base station IDs, causing the MN to waste energy scanning and sending RtSolPr messages.

The RFC recommends that the MN perform scanning to verify advertised base stations before reacting. WiMAX handover messages involved in the actual switch are authenticated using message authentication codes, so they are protected from spoofing.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone could lie about which towers are nearby, wasting the phone's battery. But the actual handover commands are signed so they cannot be faked.
